"Flowery" has two distinct lives — one literal and one figurative. You need to understand both, because people use this word in very different situations.

This is the simpler, more obvious meaning. When something is described as flowery, it means it is full of flowers, decorated with flower patterns, or smells like flowers.

This meaning has three small branches:

a) Covered with or full of flowers
If a place or surface has many flowers on it, you can call it flowery.

"We had a picnic in a flowery meadow."
"She wore a flowery dress."

b) Decorated with a flower pattern or design
Even if there are no real flowers, something printed or designed with flower shapes is called flowery.

"The old kitchen had flowery wallpaper on all the walls."
"He gave her a gift wrapped in flowery paper."

c) Smelling like flowers
A scent that reminds you of flowers — sweet, soft, and pleasant — can be called flowery.

"The shampoo had a light, flowery fragrance."
"The spring air was warm and flowery."

All three of these uses share the same spirit: they connect the thing to flowers — in appearance, design, or smell.

This is the more important and more frequently used meaning in everyday life. When people say someone's language, speech, or writing is flowery, they mean it is filled with too many fancy words, poetic phrases, long-winded expressions, and unnecessary decoration — to the point where it becomes excessive or even hard to follow.

Think of it this way: just as you can over-decorate a room with too many flowers until it feels suffocating, you can over-decorate your language with too many beautiful-sounding words until the actual meaning gets lost inside all that decoration.

"His speech was so flowery that nobody could understand what he was actually trying to say."
"She wrote a flowery letter full of poetic descriptions, but the main point was buried deep inside it."
"The politician gave a flowery answer that sounded impressive but said nothing real."

Key things to understand about this figurative meaning:

1. It almost always carries a slightly negative tone.
When you call someone's language "flowery," you are gently criticizing it. You are suggesting that the person is trying too hard to sound impressive, eloquent, or poetic — and that this effort is getting in the way of clear communication. It is not a harsh insult, but it is a criticism.

2. It is about excess, not just beauty.
Beautiful, well-chosen language is not called flowery. Flowery language specifically refers to language where someone has gone overboard — using five fancy words when one plain word would do, or decorating a simple idea with layers of dramatic metaphors and poetic phrases unnecessarily.

3. It can suggest insincerity.
Sometimes, when language is too polished and too beautifully decorated, it starts to feel fake or hollow — as if the person is more focused on sounding good than on meaning what they say. This is why "flowery praise" or "flowery compliments" can sound suspicious, as if the person is flattering you but doesn't really mean it.

"He greeted everyone with flowery compliments, but nobody trusted him."

4. The context is almost always writing or speech.
You will hear this figurative meaning applied to: letters, speeches, poetry (when it's overdone), emails, essays, song lyrics, compliments, apologies, and conversations.
The Core Contrast: Flowery vs. Plain

To truly nail this word, keep this contrast in mind:

Instead of saying...A flowery version might say...
"I like you.""Your presence fills my soul with the warmth of a thousand golden sunsets."
"He was late.""He arrived, fashionably delayed, as the clock ticked its way well past the appointed hour."
"The food was good.""Each morsel was a symphony of flavors dancing upon my grateful palate."

In each case, the flowery version is not wrong, but it is decorated far beyond what is needed. That is the heart of the figurative meaning.

• Ornate — heavily decorated (more neutral, used for both language and objects)
  • Elaborate — complex and detailed beyond what's necessary
  • Verbose — using too many words
  • Florid — very close in meaning to flowery; also describes overly fancy language or a red, flushed complexion
  • Bombastic — pompously wordy and inflated language (stronger and harsher than flowery)
The Opposite of Flowery (When Used Figuratively)

• Plain — simple, direct, no decoration
  • Direct — straight to the point
  • Concise — brief and clear
  • Simple — easy and undecorated

Flowery in its literal sense = having, showing, or smelling of flowers.

Flowery in its figurative sense = language or speech that is excessively decorated with fancy words and poetic expressions, to the point where it feels overdone, showy, or insincere. This is the more common and more important use of the word in everyday life.

When in doubt, ask yourself: "Is there too much decoration here — more than what's needed?" If yes, "flowery" is likely the right word.
